about: Questions asked of the planner. Each answer should spawn new questions; `unlocks` names the data that would answer an open one.

questions.question: Where should a new GP surgery go?
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): by walking distance, St Peters near Hidcote Close (WR5 3; ~3,900 households brought within 15 min). The earlier Norton Road answer used OpenStreetMap GPs, which missed surgeries and counted hospital clinics.

questions.question: Does being far from a GP actually harm people's health?
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): still no sign. After age and deprivation, GP walking distance shows no link with Census 2021 bad health (t = 0.8). Deprivation explains most of the difference.

questions.question: Can people actually get an appointment? Which surgeries are over capacity?
questions.unlocks: NHS Digital: patients registered per GP practice, GP workforce (FTE GPs per practice)
questions.finding: Partly, without GP staff numbers (not published where we can reach it). 9 practices serve Worcester, all large (6,900–21,900 patients; England's typical practice ~8,800). Patients finding the wait acceptable (GP Patient Survey 2024, England 66%): Haresfield House 55%, St Martin's Gate 58%, St Johns House 59%, up to Spring Gardens 84%. Pressure by geography (residents whose nearest surgery it is, vs its registered list): Elbury Moor 31,700 vs 12,400; Spring Gardens 27,300 vs 20,100; St Johns House 19,900 vs 13,800.

questions.question: Why is health worst around Selsey Close and Windermere Drive, when a GP is 12–18 min away?
questions.unlocks: Index of Multiple Deprivation (income, employment, housing), access to green space, fast-food density, air quality

questions.question: Do older people in Lower Wick (35% over 65, 38 min walk to a GP) have a bus or car to get there?
questions.unlocks: Census 2021 car availability (TS045); bus timetables (Bus Open Data) for real public-transport times
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): Lower Wick (012E) is 27 min from a GP on foot, ~25 by bus or walking. 15% of households have no car; only 11% have a frequent bus stop within 5 min.

questions.question: Should 'best site' be ranked by need (health, age, deprivation) instead of just households within walking distance?
questions.unlocks: A need score per neighbourhood from data already loaded; change rankChanges to weight by need
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): ranking by need still moves the answer: the top need-weighted GP sites are Bath Road and Nunnery Lane in St Peters, and Winchcombe Drive in the Warndon Villages. (Before the correction it pointed to Malvern Road, St John's, but Severn Valley Medical Practice, the town's largest, is already there.)

questions.question: How often do buses actually run from Lower Wick to a GP surgery?
questions.unlocks: Bus Open Data GTFS timetables (West Midlands, 207 MB, reachable): trips per hour and journey times to each surgery
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): buses help a little. Lower Wick: GP 27 min walking, ~25 by bus or walking; only 11% near a frequent stop. Town-wide, buses cut the average GP trip from 22 to 18 min; 54% of households have a stop with 4+ buses an hour within 5 min.

questions.question: Is the west side (St John's, Dines Green, Lower Wick) cut off by the River Severn, with too few crossings?
questions.unlocks: Detour ratios already computed (access.js) split by river side; count of walkable and drivable crossings; traffic counts on the crossings
questions.finding: Corrected 28 Oct 2026 with official NHS practices (gps.json): the river matters less than it first looked. West bank 26 min to a GP on average, east bank 20.5 (earlier 31 vs 16 came from missing west-bank surgeries and hospital clinics counted as GPs on the east). 6 walkable crossings, 2 for cars; the best new footbridge saves under a minute per household.

questions.question: Why do corner shops seem to do better in poorer neighbourhoods, and the opposite in well-off ones?
questions.finding: Partly true, weakly. The most deprived third of Worcester's neighbourhoods has ~1.7x the convenience shops per household (0.96 vs 0.58 per 1,000) and 2x the supermarkets. The likelier driver is car ownership, not money as such: 33% of households there have no car vs 11% in the least deprived third. Only 30 convenience shops are mapped in OSM, so treat as a hint.

questions.question: Are corner shops thriving or just surviving, and what else (takeaways, cafes, pubs) clusters with deprivation and bad health?
questions.unlocks: Food Standards Agency hygiene ratings API (reachable): every food business with type and location; opening and closing dates over time
questions.finding: Food Standards Agency register (546 food businesses in Worcester; 111 small food shops vs 30 in OpenStreetMap). Leaving out the 2 city-centre neighbourhoods: small food shops are ~3.5x as common in the most deprived third (2.37 vs 0.67 per 1,000 households), and track households without a car (r = 0.36) a little more than deprivation (0.32). Takeaways show no link with deprivation (r = 0.02) or bad health (-0.03) in Worcester, against the usual assumption. Whether shops are thriving or just surviving needs openings and closures over time.

questions.question: What should happen to County Hall, Worcester?
questions.unlocks: Site size and condition; planning.data.gov.uk (local plan, constraints, listed status); access scores for the site as homes vs offices vs a health hub; traffic on Spetchley Road; Worcestershire County Council's own estate plans
questions.progress: Scenarios (scenarios/*.json, scored by `npm run planner -- scenarios`): a health hub at County Hall lifts the town score +0.8 and cuts the average GP walk by 1.2 min. 600 homes alone (an illustrative number) would leave the new residents ~30 min from a GP (shop 7, school 10.5); homes + hub fixes that (+1.2 overall). But a surgery at Bath Road, St Peters, does more for existing residents (+1.7; GP walk -2.8 min, need-weighted -1.7). Still open: site size and condition, the council's plans, traffic on Spetchley Road. Who gains: a County Hall hub saves 6,620 households ~10 min to a GP (607 without a car); a Bath Road surgery saves 7,877 households ~19 min (744 without a car).

questions.question: What should we do with Worcester's empty shops?
questions.unlocks: Where they are: OSM vacant/disused shop tags (patchy), FSA closures, Valuation Office business rates list, council vacancy surveys; footfall proxies (bus stops, car parks, traffic counts); what similar towns did
questions.progress: 35 empty shops are mapped in OpenStreetMap (a lower bound; volunteers record them unevenly): ~27 in the city centre around High Street, Foregate Street and Crowngate, including the former Debenhams and Ernest Jones (checked Aug 2025); Carpetright at Blackpole; and a former Costcutter on Ambleside Drive, Warndon. Shown as grey dots. Still open: an official vacancy count (business rates / council surveys) and what each unit could become, tested as scenarios.

questions.question: What would a 'New Worcester' look like, cyclist-friendly vs driver-friendly?
questions.unlocks: Scenarios as sets of network edits, scored on one dashboard (access, traffic, cycling, health benefit via WHO HEAT, safety via STATS19). Ties together q7, q8, q11, q12
questions.progress: Scenario tool built: a scenario is a named set of changes (new places, homes, roads) scored on one scorecard against Worcester today (access score, share within targets, walk and bus-or-walk minutes, need-weighted GP walk, and the new homes' own access). First four scenarios are about County Hall and St Peters. Cycling and car-free changes need a mode-choice model next.

questions.question: Could a west-bank health hub work at or near Malvern Road, St John's: is there a building or site, and do buses reach it?
questions.unlocks: planning.data.gov.uk brownfield land and sites; empty commercial buildings in St John's (links to q12); Bus Open Data timetables from Lower Wick, Dines Green and Henwick (links to q7); NHS practice list sizes for the existing west-bank surgeries (links to q3)
questions.progress: Location checks out on access: a GP at Malvern Road cuts Lower Wick (012E) from 38 to ~16 min walking and the west bank's average from 31 to 24 min. Still open: a building or site, and capacity of the existing west-bank surgeries.
questions.finding: Withdrawn: it rested on OpenStreetMap missing Severn Valley Medical Practice (21,893 patients), which already sits in St John's.

questions.question: Which neighbourhoods have the worst bus service for their need (old, no car, deprived) and where would one more frequent route help most?
questions.unlocks: bus.json (frequency per stop, bus-or-walk minutes per neighbourhood) + need score already loaded; route shapes from the GTFS shapes.txt to test a rerouted or extra service

questions.question: Is St Peters really without a GP within reach (41 min walk around Foxglove Road), or do branch surgeries fill the gap?
questions.unlocks: Branch surgery sites (NHS ODS branch codes, practice websites); where St Peters residents are actually registered (practice-to-LSOA registration counts, NHS Digital)

questions.question: Why is Elbury Moor the nearest surgery for ~31,700 people but registers 12,400? Where do Warndon's residents actually go?
questions.unlocks: Patients registered by LSOA per practice (NHS Digital, blocked from this cloud box: needs another route or a local run)

questions.question: Are Worcester's corner shops opening or closing, and does losing one hurt households without a car?
questions.unlocks: FSA register snapshots over time (new and removed businesses), Companies House dissolutions, OSM disused:shop tags; a scenario that removes a shop and scores the households without a car around it
questions.finding: For the one closed corner shop mapped (former Costcutter, Ambleside Drive, Warndon: the worst-health neighbourhood, half of households without a car), reopening it brings 289 households a shop an average 1.4 min closer, 71 of them without a car. Other small shops nearby cover most of the loss by distance; price and range may matter more and aren't in this data. Openings and closures over time still need FSA snapshots.

questions.question: Who finds everyday life hardest to reach, and are they the people who need it most?
questions.finding: Answered by a plan of tools (plans/everyday-access-and-need.json), no new code. Need goes with shorter distances (t = -4.7): the most deprived, car-less neighbourhoods are nearer everyday services. The hardest to reach are newer suburbs: St Peters, Henwick, Perdiswell, the Warndon Villages, Lower Wick. Car-less households: GP 14 min by bus or walking vs 18.6 for all.

questions.question: What can Old Worcester teach New Worcester? Did services follow growth, and how did travel change?
questions.finding: Neighbourhoods built up since 1995 are further from everyday life (t = 2.3 after deprivation and age): Worcester grew outward without services. Driving to work rose 71% -> 76% (2011 -> 2021, lockdown caveat), bus halved, cycling and walking fell. Perdiswell, Barbourne and Dines Green have everyday life close but still drive 71-83%: first places for walking and cycling. Recorded as lessons L1-L4 in NEW_WORCESTER.md.

questions.question: How many people in Perdiswell and Barbourne would walk or cycle if routes were safer and quicker?
questions.unlocks: A travel-choice tool: Census 2021 travel to work by distance band (TS058) and origin-destination flows, Propensity to Cycle Tool scenarios, cycle route network from OSM, collision data (STATS19) for safety

questions.question: Can people in Worcester have a good ordinary day within reach: somewhere to meet, green space, food and a GP?
questions.finding: 32% of households have all four (meeting place <= 10 min, green <= 5, food <= 10, GP <= 15 walking or bus). GP is the bottleneck (48%), then green space (58%). Car-less households 47%, over-65s 27%. St Peters and the Warndon Villages have none; the centre has most. Need goes with a good day (t = 5.3). 96% of households are outside flood zones; riverside St Clements has 21% in Zone 3.

questions.question: What would a good day look like for real kinds of residents: an older person without a car in Lower Wick, a young family in St Peters, a home-worker in Barbourne?
questions.unlocks: Personas built from census profiles (age, household, car, work), a day's trips through the model (tools: travel, busOrWalk), time with others vs time travelling; then the same days in each New Worcester scenario

questions.question: Which single change would give the most St Peters and Warndon Villages households a good day within reach?
questions.unlocks: Score scenarios on the good-day share, not just GP minutes: a GP, a meeting place, a pocket park, a frequent bus, each tested with compare + meets

questions.question: How safe is Worcester city centre once crime is measured per visitor or per job, not per resident?
questions.unlocks: Jobs per neighbourhood (have) as a denominator; footfall or visitor counts (BID/council counters); crime by type and hour
questions.progress: Per 1,000 residents + workers, Fort Royal is still well above expected (322 vs 134). Shoppers and visitors aren't counted yet; footfall data would settle it.

questions.question: A quarter of households in St John's (009E) and the Arboretum (007A) are one person over 66, with meeting places under 4 minutes away. Do those places suit older people, and who checks in?
questions.unlocks: Kinds of meeting place within reach (community centre, library, lunch club, place of worship vs pub), opening hours, step-free access; Age UK / council befriending services

questions.question: Why is health in Warndon & Elbury Park (005A) worse than its deprivation and age predict?
questions.unlocks: Census disability and long-term conditions (TS038), air quality near the M5 and Parsonage Way, Fingertips GP practice prevalence (QOF) for Elbury Moor

questions.question: Why do St John's and the Arboretum cycle more than expected while Nunnery cycles far less, and why did cycling fall everywhere 2011-2021?
questions.unlocks: Cycle network (have) along each area's route to the centre, hills (terrain), busy-road crossings, collisions involving cyclists (STATS19 casualty file), census 2021 lockdown effect

questions.question: Which of the survey's links survive once the centre's few residents and many visitors are allowed for?
questions.unlocks: Re-run the survey without the two centre neighbourhoods, or with residents + jobs as the denominator
questions.finding: Re-run two ways (plans/survey-centre-fair.json): per 1,000 residents + workers, and per resident without the two centre neighbourhoods. The corner shops / pubs / takeaways / crime links (~0.9) vanish: they were the centre's few residents. Surviving both: crime and violence with car-less households and deprivation (0.7-0.8), bad health with deprivation (0.87), income (-0.69) and violence (0.65), car-less households where homes are cheaper, good day with GP access (-0.85), living alone with age (0.81).

questions.question: Why does Leopard Hill (008A, around Nine Acres Green) record four times the violent crime its deprivation predicts? One place or the neighbourhood?
questions.unlocks: Crime points within the area (police.uk snap points: are most at one location?), what's there (a venue, hostel, custody or care setting), by month

questions.question: Shoplifting drives crime in Rainbow Hill and the Warndon local centre. Should shop crime be mapped apart from crime against residents?
questions.unlocks: Split crime.json by category into 'against people/homes' (violence, burglary, ASB, damage) and 'against businesses' (shoplifting); re-run the survey

questions.question: Where does immigration fit in Worcester's whole picture: health, money, crime, services, housing?
questions.finding: Census per neighbourhood: 12.8% born abroad, 6% arrived 2011-21. They live where homes are cheaper and fewer have cars. Raw link to crime (0.51) vanishes once car-less households and deprivation are allowed for (t 0.8); same for violence and health. Home Office asylum support: 78 people (June 2026), half England's rate per head. Small boats: national only, not mappable.

questions.question: Do recent arrivals reach a GP, English classes and work as well as everyone else nearby? Where are ESOL classes, and are they walkable from Fort Royal, Arboretum and Warndon 005B?
questions.unlocks: ESOL class locations (college, library, community listings) as a place kind; GP registration of new arrivals isn't published per practice

questions.question: Is Worcester growing mainly from people moving in (from the UK and abroad) or from births? What does that mean for homes, schools and GP lists by 2035?
questions.unlocks: ONS mid-year population estimates with components of change (births, deaths, internal and international migration) for the council, 2011-2025

questions.question: What is different around Windermere Drive (Warndon & Elbury Park 005A): child poverty, health, obesity, self-harm and crime all well above what its deprivation predicts?
questions.unlocks: Housing mix (social rent, overcrowding), services within reach, youth and family services, what residents report (FixMyStreet), council housing data
questions.finding: Spotlight (plans/spotlight-warndon.json): not a services gap. Walks to GP, shops, parks and meeting places are about average and half of workers travel under 5 km. It is poverty, housing and health: bottom 6% for income after housing and healthy life expectancy (58 vs 66), top 6% for child poverty (48%) and early deaths, 43% social rent, overcrowding double, a third without a car, 23% turnout. 003A is a better-off corner; the estate is 002A-D and 005A/B/F.

questions.question: Why do people in Dines Green & Grove Farm live three years longer than their deprivation predicts? What can other neighbourhoods copy?
questions.unlocks: Green space and countryside edge, air, community groups (charities register), age mix, GP practice
questions.progress: Spotlight: cleanest air in the city (bottom 3% for NO2), fewest hazards on the healthy-places index (bottom 9%), countryside edge (every home within 1 km of a nature reserve); also fast-growing (+39% since 2011) and few charities. Fits L24; the residents' own view is missing.

questions.question: Which streets would cleaner air help most? Where do the busiest roads run past homes, schools and GP surgeries?
questions.unlocks: Road traffic counts and noise maps beside homes; Defra roadside model; school locations

questions.question: Worcester is ageing fast (65+ up 32% since 2011, children flat). Where will older residents live in 2035, and can they reach a GP, a bus and a meeting place without a car?
questions.unlocks: Population projections by age, care homes, step-free access, bus stops near homes of over-65s
questions.finding: plans/older-residents.json: 65+ grew fastest (more than doubled since 2011) in the 1990s car suburbs: Warndon Villages (St Nicholas), Leopard Hill, St Peter's, Diglis. They have the least within reach for older people: a good day is 0% of over-65s in St Peter's, 3% St Nicholas, 6% St Clement, 10% Battenhall (city 30%). Over-65s take 20 min to a GP against 18 for all.

questions.question: How often is the Severn at Worcester unsafe to swim or row after rain, and where do people use it?
questions.unlocks: Storm overflow start/stop times (2025 detailed EDM), river use (rowing clubs, swimming spots), rainfall

questions.question: Why is fuel poverty in Worcester (14% of homes) so much higher than in Gloucester and Cheltenham (9%), at similar deprivation to Gloucester?
questions.unlocks: Energy certificates (EPC, needs a free account: Harry's call), house age and type (council tax bands), off-gas-grid homes

questions.question: Worcester has the most people on GP depression registers and the highest anxiety of the three towns, yet the fewest self-harm admissions. Is it more distress, or better recording and care?
questions.unlocks: Antidepressant prescribing per practice (NHSBSA), talking-therapy referrals, wellbeing in more years

questions.question: Why is Worcester the only one of the three losing children since 2011? Where did young families go?
questions.unlocks: Population by age per neighbourhood over time, new-build homes by size, school rolls, house prices against local wages

questions.question: What would help the Warndon estate most that a planner controls: cheaper, warmer homes; a GP or health hub with longer hours; youth and family space; better buses to jobs; or a stronger say? Which have worked elsewhere?
questions.unlocks: Evidence from similar estates (e.g. Marmot places, Big Local areas), council housing stock and repairs, GP opening hours and list per GP, youth services, bus frequency to the main job sites

questions.question: Why is turnout so low where need is highest, and does it change when people are asked directly (community panels, door-step consultations)?
questions.unlocks: Turnout history per ward (Democracy Club), council consultation response rates by area, registration rates

questions.question: Worcester's food help is two sites in the centre. Would a food bank point or community pantry west of the Severn (Dines Green, St Clement, Lower Wick: 25-29 minutes away by walk or bus) reach people the centre doesn't?
questions.unlocks: Bus or walk minutes from each neighbourhood to the two sites (travel tool, food bank as a place kind), food bank referral numbers by postcode district if the food bank shares them, Your Local Pantry model
questions.progress: plans/foodbank-reach.json: average 24 minutes (Gloucester 24, Cheltenham 21) because buses converge on the centre; the Warndon estate is 18 minutes; the west bank is the gap, as for GPs (L8).

questions.question: What would give older residents of St Peter's and Warndon Villages a good day without a car: a small health and community hub, a demand-responsive bus, a corner shop in a vacant unit, or benches and safer crossings on the walk? Which reaches most for least?
questions.unlocks: Scenario: add a hub (GP + café + meeting room) at St Peter's district centre or Warndon Villages and score over-65 good day; bus timetables on those estates by hour; step-free routes
questions.progress: plans/older-residents-hubs.json: three small hubs (St Peter's centre, Warndon Villages, Battenhall) take over-65 good day from 3% to 46% (St Nicholas), 10% to 50% (Battenhall), 0% to 37% (St Peter's); city-wide 30% to 35%. Still to test: a demand-responsive bus, a shop in a vacant unit, benches and crossings. plans/older-residents-options.json (L31): shop or meeting room alone +0; GP room alone 30% to 34%; full hub 35%; a 30% slower walk (no benches or crossings) drops it to 16%; a door-to-door bus to GP and shops 61% at most.
